Westfield Innovation · Season 28 · Soft goods

We stopped drawing bags. We started building them.

Twenty volumetric forms, modelled as solids, printed at 1:5 scale and judged by hand — before anyone drew a single flat.

20 modelled · 3 printed · 2 sampled · TB4695-20L Diamond · TB4696-22L Spiral

01 — First, the volume

Twenty solids, before a single flat.

SPIRALDIAMOND

Real geometry, not renderings. Each was modelled to be judged as a volume — proportion, tension, how the panels break across the body — on the questions a drawing cannot answer.

02 — Then, the object

Three came off the printer. A week in people's hands settled it.

Printed at 1:5, passed around, turned over and argued about. Structural viability and immediate visual appeal — judgements a screen will not give you honestly.

Eighteen forms were killed on a table · the cheapest place to kill anything

→ DIAMOND
→ SPIRAL
NOT CARRIED

03 — The two that survived

Diamond and Spiral.

Diamond · TB4695-20L

A structured body of mirrored triangular panels, M-profile lower webbing and a slanted access zipper across the front face.

Spiral · TB4696-22L

A sling-and-pack hybrid. One panel wraps from the front face down into the hip, so the pack and the belt are one piece.

Form study 14 and form study 9 · the shape argument was over

06 — What this changes for soft goods

Form is a decision, not a discovery.

Model, don't sketch

Twenty solids cost a week of sprint time and settled the shape before anything was committed to.

Print before you spec

A form you can hold gets an honest answer. Three prints replaced an argument nobody wins on a screen.

Draw what exists

The tech pack stops being a proposal and becomes a description. Nothing is left to interpret.

Then detail it

Sample notes came back about pockets, mesh and webbing. Never the silhouette.

“Get the shape and construction down first” · Timber Ridge Daypack spec pack, April 2026
